maintopic: RENEWAL OF MOST FAVOURED NATION AGREEMENT WITH BULGARIA

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: RENEWAL OF MOST FAVOURED NATION AGREEMENT WITH BULGARIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the house that we have reached agreement with the People's Republic of Bulgaria to renew the most favoured nation trade agreement between our two countries. The appropriate documents will be signed later today.
Mr. Dimitar Kostov, chairman of the Bulgarian trade delegation, is in Ottawa to sign on behalf of his government the agreement which brings to a successful conclusion talks I opened with the Bulgarian trade minister, Mr. Budinov, in Sofia last September. The negotiations carried forward the friendly spirit of cooperation which has been a feature of our trade relations with Bulgaria in recent years.
Under the terms of the agreement Bulgaria has undertaken to purchase a minimum of 7.4 million bushels of wheat during the next three years with an option on a further 3.7 million bushels subject to the ability of the Canadian Wheat Board to supply. The basic quantity together with the additional option would represent about $24 million of trade at current prices. Purchases of wheat will be facilitated by the extension of credit arrangements under the Export Credits Insurance Act providing for payment over three years.
[DOT] (11:10 a.m.)
The exchange of letters concerning the expansion and diversification of trade between Canada and Bulgaria will express the interest of both contracting parties in further developing trade between our two countries. Bulgaria undertakes to give first consideration to Canada as a competitive source of supply for a number of goods other than wheat for which Canada has demonstrated export performance. The letter also indicates that within the framework of the laws and regulations it should be possible for Bulgaria to expand its exports to Canada.

speechtext: To the knowledge of the government, has the legislature of the province of Quebec established an administrative procedure for dealing with other governments and, if so, what is the policy of the government toward it?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: WRITTEN QUESTIONS AND MOTIONS FOR PAPERS
subtopic: QUEBEC-PROCEDURE FOR DEALING WITH OTHER GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
The government is aware that Bill 33 entitled "An act to amend the federal-provincial affairs department act and certain related acts" was adopted by the Quebec legislature on April 13, 1967. In answer to questions raised in this house at the time when that bill was read for the first time in the Quebec legislature, I stated on behalf of the government, that to the extent that this legislation purported to set up the administrative machinery which the Quebec government felt it required for the performance of the functions assigned to its competence, this was a matter for the Quebec government to decide.
Since then, however, the government has had occasion to see the legislation in question, and to follow the debates on it in the Quebec legislature. Due note has been taken of statements made on that occasion that the sole purpose of this legislation was to effect an internal transfer and reorganization of existing administrative functions and responsibilities. However, a certain ambiguity of wording in parts of the legislation has resulted in interpretations by the press and elsewhere as possibly having the effect of entrusting this new department with responsibilities in the
[Mr. Gregoire.l
external field such as for relations between Quebec and foreign countries, and for the negotiation of agreements with foreign governments or bodies.
There should be no ground for any such misunderstanding.
The constitutional position in Canada with respect to the division of powers as between the federal and provincial governments clearly gives the federal government exclusive responsibility for the conduct of the country's external affairs. This cannot be altered by legislation adopted by a provincial legislature. Quebec legislation cannot confer upon the government of Quebec any of the powers which are now assigned exclusively by the constitution to the federal government for the conduct of Canada's relations with foreign countries and for the negotiation and conclusion of agreements with these countries in all fields. The government of Quebec is of course aware of these constitutional requirements in the field of external affairs and there is no reason to believe that the manner in which the new Quebec department will carry out the functions assigned to it by this bill will not be fully consistent with the constitutional position in Canada.
With regard to Quebec provincial agents abroad, whose responsibility is assigned by this new legislation to the department of intergovernmental affairs, it is a well known fact that provincial agencies abroad-which have existed for many years-do not form part of the Canadian diplomatic and consular establishment in foreign countries. Thus they are not empowered to exercise abroad any of the functions which, within our constitutional framework and in accordance with international practice, it is the exclusive responsibility of Canadian diplomatic and consular missions abroad to perform on behalf of all of Canada. Consequently the role of these agencies does not consist in transacting with foreign governmental authorities official business affecting Canada or any part thereof in any field unless agreement has been reached beforehand through diplomatic channels between the Canadian government and the foreign government concerned on the matters to be transacted with provincial authorities and the manner in which this is to be done.
April 26, 1967

The hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) suggested in a strong outburst yesterday, that we were proposing to interfere with the workers' freedom.
In my answer to the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacDonald) I mentioned that workers would not be free to pick one course in preference to another because the fear expressed by the hon. member for Prince was that, at a given moment, the worker might choose a longer course simply because he would get more allowances from the federal government. I mentioned to him that the manpower centre would then have the authority to refuse if there was abuse.
The member for Lapointe obviously said he was scandalized, claiming that we infringed upon the freedom of the workers.
The workers are just as free as any other citizens but no more. This means that, for instance, everybody is not being admitted to university at this time, for there are conditions to be met, not only educational qualifications but also available space. The same thing has to apply in the field of manpower too, that is to say, if a worker wants occupational training which is not worthwhile and which will not increase his future income and his opportunities for employment, the manpower centre will certainly not agree to pay allowances in such a case. The worker remains free to follow such courses if he wishes, but we will be free to pay because if there is unemployment in a specific trade or in a specific town, it certainly would not be sensible for the manpower centre to train new people for this trade or profession.
There is a conditioning to freedom which must not only be explained but also motivated.
Therefore, I suggest it is exaggerated to object that this manpower centre was to force a trade or a profession upon somebody and, if that can have some effect in certain quarters, I think that here, in this house, there should be no misunderstanding about the scope of such charges.

This does not mean that these people are ready to operate overnight, but we are trying to upgrade our own staff. The staff has very important responsibilities, and this program can be a success if we do have good men in the right places; I entirely agree with the hon. member there.
[DOT] (12 noon)

Therefore, in closing, I will deal with the objections raised by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire). In short, if a demand exists in a trade or two and if a worker indicates a preference and is qualified, there is no doubt that we would then take his preference into account. But if he is not qualified or if the trade is congested or no longer exists, of course the manpower centre will not accept to pay an allowance to that worker who will want, for instance, to learn the trade of piano tuner in a village where there is not a single piano.
That has nothing to do with restricting freedom, it is simply being realistic and trying to orient manpower properly.
Of course, the desire and that freedom are conditioned also by the individual's qualifications. For instance, if someone who wants to become an airplane pilot is blind in one eye, it is not interfering with his freedom to tell him that he cannot take the course.
[Mr. Lewis.)
At any rate, let us say that there is an abuse of the word "freedom" simply to make trouble.
The second serious objection, or apparently serious, which was raised by the hon. member for Lapointe had to do with overlapping of services and double taxation, I took the trouble yesterday to explain to him precisely how that situation could occur previously and how, under the new system, there was really no division between the two functions, that of education which is entirely provincial and that of the federal government which is to help financially the workers who need to be retrained.
If tomorrow the province would assume the federal responsibility, it would have to hire the same people who are working for us at the present time. Therefore, there is no double taxation, no overlapping of services. The province pays for the education, the province manages its institutions and it has inspectors for those institutions. Of course, we shall have accountants to audit the expenditures.
However, if that jurisdiction were left with the province, tomorrow morning it would have to hire people to perform that task.

There is no double taxation, no duplication of services. It is very clearly defined. There is double taxation and duplication of services when two governments are trying to cover the same field at the same time. This can occur, for instance, in loan insurance cases. If the provincial and federal governments are both insuring the same loans and levying from the taxpayers a tax for that purpose, there is really double taxation there, since the same service is being taxed twice.
And I believe, Mr. Chairman, that the best example of double taxation is, no doubt, the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), who was elected to represent his constituents in the field of federal jurisdiction, but is simply coming here in order to discuss problems coming under provincial jurisdiction. Now, there is already a provincial member in Quebec. And this means that the Lapointe people are being taxed double for the same service.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose I was dealing with some of the difficulties which I see still existing in the implementation of this bill. I was dealing with one of the major objections the minister had to my earlier comments, and I suppose to the comments of every hon. member who has spoken, namely, that we were repeating as if they were completely true the questions that have been raised by the provincial governments, mainly, the minister suggested, by the province of Ontario.
April 26, 1967

I now want to deal with another matter which was dealt with by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris and several other hon. members, namely, the problems which will arise in the implementation of this bill as it relates to the training of a particular group, Indians.
It is true that the minister has expressed some very fine sentiments to the effect that Indians would not be treated any differently from other people in the community. That sounds very good except for the fact that Indians are different from other people in the community. They are different for two reasons. First of all, under our constitution Indians are the responsibility of the federal government. So we have a greater responsibility for them than for any other people in Canada. They are also different because the level of education of the Indian is vastly below the level of education of the population of Canada as a whole. It is for that reason that the clauses of the bill spelling out that the provisions of the program will not be applicable to those people who are at least one year older than the regular school leaving age and the provision with respect to being three years in the work force will, I suggest to the minister, have a catastrophic effect upon the training of Indians.
I suggest to the minister that he stop thinking about what is implicit in everything he has said since the debate began, namely, that the criticisms being made by members on this side of the house are to a large extent of a political nature. Of course all of us here are politicians, and those of us in the opposition like to be able to criticize the government. However, I suggest to the minister that he pay very close attention to a submission which apparently was sent to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development by the Indian-Eskimo Association. He should pay particular attention to it not only because the association is a very responsible one but because the letter was signed by the executive director, Ernest McEwen, and the vice president, Mr. Martin P. O'Connell, of the Indian-Eskimo Association.
The minister is a relative newcomer to politics and may not know who Martin P. O'Connell is. Therefore I should like to take a few seconds to tell him that Martin O'Connell is one of the very bright people the former minister of finance brought to Ottawa to help him prepare that notorious budget which got the former minister into such trouble. Martin O'Connell was a Liberal candidate in the last election for the constituency of Greenwood
Occupational Training
where he ran against my deskmate and colleague. So no one can accuse Mr. O'Connell, when he writes a letter about the possible effects of this bill on the Indian population, of being politically antagonistic to this government.
I should like to refer to a short article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of yesterday's date. The heading is "Group Fears Indians Deprived Under Job Law" and the article reads:
The Indian-Eskimo Association of Canada is worried that Canada's new manpower training law will deprive thousands of unemployed and under-employed Indians of job training.
Martin P. O'Connell, vice-president, and Ernest McEwen, executive director of the association, said yesterday that a letter is going to Indian Affairs and Northern Development Minister Arthur Laing asking for information.
They said the letter was prompted by these facts: New regulations specify that single persons must be out of school for at least 12 months and must be at least 17 before they can take training. Single trainees must have been substantially in the labour force for three years before they can receive training allowances of $35 a week. Trainees who have dependants may draw training allowances if they are 17 and out of school for 12 months.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
More than one-third of Indians are unemployed and many never enter the labor force. A recent survey showed that 61 per cent of a large sample group of breadwinners work less than six months a year.
Large numbers of Indian children drop out of school before the age of 16.
These facts are correct. I suggest that those who have dropped out of school before reaching thei age of 16 are precisely those who ought to be encouraged to take courses so they may do useful and productive work.
When one visits the slum area of any Canadian city one notices the large numbers of such people living on welfare, idling, drinking and becoming entangled with the law. These people and others like them are excluded from the program by its rigidity. I urge the minister to heed the editorial in today's Globe and Mail and not to throw out the baby with the bath water. The minister ought to be less rigid and more accommodating in meeting the legitimate suggestions, criticisms and desires which have been expressed by all provinces.
Constitutional difficulties lead to a division of manpower training and general education, but for our population to benefit most the division ought to be abolished. Winnipeg inaugurated last year a most imaginative program whereby adults who during their school days dropped out of high school before completing their education may return to school to

April 26, 1967
Occupational Training
finish their high school training. It is difficult, as the minister knows, for anyone without a sound education to get a good job. The people of Winnipeg were surprised that the enrolment in the adult school was more than double that anticipated for any one year.
The minister alleges that education is a provincial responsibility, but I suggest that the minister's program is the most suitable vehicle for upgrading people's educational qualifications to the point where they can get better jobs. Instead of saying that the federal government will not participate in such provincial matters the minister ought to consult with the provinces to encourage the kind of educational program I spoke of. And Winnipeg is not the only city with problems. I am informed that out of a population of approximately 260,000 in the Ottawa area, 90,000 adults have not been educated beyond grade 5. One third of Ottawa's adults are poorly educated.
The minister has been in the labour movement long enough to know that it is almost impossible for a poorly educated man to find a good job. The provinces and municipalities ought to be induced to do something to improve people's education and prepare them to take the courses outlined in the program. The federal government ought to encourage such thinking. The division which has been created between education and manpower training is not only impractical but will lead to disaster for this country. I hope that in future the minister and the government will reconsider some of the principles which have been enunciated.

I ask the minister whether, in the administration of the legislation, the different pay rates in the various areas in which applicants live will be considered. There is some flexibility, but the minimum rate must be $35 and the maximum must be $90. Each province may possibly have a scale for each of its different regions. The minister and the government should have brought this bill before the house prior to March 31 instead of resorting to passing an act of parliament by regulations, and they did not merely pass regulations. This is what I object to. It is not only improper and its legality questionable but in its practical effect it is an evil thing to do. It creates doubts, misunderstandings, difficulties, misgivings, divisions and conflicts where none would have been had the government and the minister acted in accordance with their duty to parliament and the people of Canada in this regard.
The specific point I raise with the minister is this. He said in a statement published in the press and he also said on the floor of the house that the three years in the labour force

which the next clause requires is not three years service in the Canadian labour force necessarily but could be three years in the labour force of some other country from which an immigrant has come. With the greatest respect, that is an interpretation of law that is a little strange to me. I assumed from the language of the bill that, unless specifically said to be otherwise, the situations we were talking about applied to this country. We understood, and I think everybody understood, that when the minister talked about three years in the labour force he was talking about the labour force in Canada.
If the minister intends it to be otherwise, may I suggest to him that he consider including in clause 2 a definition of labour force. This could easily be done simply by stating that labour force or service in a labour force, whichever language his advisers choose to use, means not only service in a labour force in Canada but in a labour force in any other country from which an immigrant to Canada has come. If he does that I think he will allay a great deal of the fear that some of his manpower officers may interpret this legislation in a narrow way.

Mr. Chairman, as I stated, this is surely what is intended. I have no objection to making this change if it can be made, so I will make a note of it and see whether the bill can be amended along these lines.

In order to test the application of this bill I should like to put a question relating to a specific situation which has recently come to my attention. It has to do with a young man 23 years of age who is married and has two children. He has had some difficulty in securing the kind of work he would like to do. For a time he lived in my constituency, and this is the reason he telephoned me.
On exploring his educational qualifications and so on it appeared that he was really

interested in a teaching career and specifically a teaching career in northern Canada. I suggested that he go to the manpower office and make inquiries about this, which he did. He was referred to someone in the education section of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, where he was told that he should take a teacher training course or normal school course in the province of Ontario and come back and see them again. Without going into the question whether this legislation is already in effect by regulation, I point out that this example is of recent date.
Therefore I address my question to the minister in the form of this specific example in the hope that he will make clearer than he has so far done what he means when he says that there are no occupational exclusions under this plan. Mr. Chairman, so far as the example given is concerned I think I told the hon. member for Brandon-Souris this morning that if a person wants to teach a trade which falls under the definition of this law he is entitled to allowances and to all the benefits of this legislation. If the hon. member wants a definition of occupational training, it is defined in clause 2 in terms of time. An occupational training course originally meant a course of occupational training not more than 12 months in duration. That has now been amended to read as follows:
(d) "occupational training course" means a course of occupational training that provides not more than fifty-two weeks of full-time instruction or 1,820 hours of part-time instruction;
That is the amendment that was proposed. We have added the number of hours, that is all.

Mr. Chairman, as I understand the bill the minister still has not clarified the situation. I have referred to clause 2 where "occupational training" specifically excludes instruction designed for

Suppose a man wants to go to northern Canada as a teacher under the northern education program to teach mathematics or English or history or languages. Is he disqualified under this plan whereas if he was going to teach metal work or drafting or something of that kind he would not be?

That is the way I read the bill. If the man in the example I quoted wishes to teach certain subjects he may qualify. Is that correct? I speak of a man who says, "I am married, with two children and I cannot afford to take one year in normal school." Yet this man is a graduate of high school with one year at university behind him. That qualifies him for normal school. Will the manpower officer be able to say to this man who wants to teach: "Yes, if your lack of training in this field is stopping you from getting a job teaching in the north we can pay you a training allowance while you go to normal school for ten months?"

Perhaps I have not made myself clear. I said that there is no occupational restriction. I do not think there are any. The only limitation is that we do not cover university training or training exceeding one year. That is all. Outside that everything is covered in the bill.
Can the minister not tell me whether the person I referred to could take a ten month course under this plan at normal school?

reliance that is entitled to be placed on the act but, with respect, what the hon. gentleman asks is not part of my job.

Mr. Chairman, I have only one question to put to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand).
Yesterday, during the debate, I reminded him that, about a month ago, officials from the Quebec government came to Ottawa-I do not know whether they met the minister, but probably his officials-to discuss this federal legislation and probably also to explain the intention of the Quebec government to legislate or occupy completely or partially this field of occupational training.
That quick visit took place about a month ago and editorialists even talked about the eventuality of a crisis-but I would not subscribe to that because I am in favour of eliminating all crises-but I would like the minister to tell us whether himself or his officials agreed with the Quebec government on the characteristics of the federal act and the role or intentions of the provincial government in the field of occupational training of adults.

Mr. Chairman, I have not discussed nor to my knowledge has anyone in my department discussed the intentions of the provincial government. Mr. Chairman, if it were not for the program we have before us today I would be tempted to make a longer speech on this subject. As it is, I wish to move an amendment to this clause and explain to the minister with all the non-partisanship I can muster the reason for this amendment. If he could tell me that it is not necessary the situation would be different.
Other members of the party to which I have the honour to belong have stressed our unhappiness at the introduction into this legislation of the Trudeau-Marchand-Pearson interpretation of the Canadian constitutional scene. The sudden refusal by the government last fall to accept a proposition upon which it had previously acted, namely, that there is a province in this country which occupies a particular place because of its function as the headquarters of French Canadian culture, has led the government to adopt policies which necessarily mean the eventual erosion of the influence of the government of Canada on important developments across this country.
In the bill before us the minister has produced what I believe to be an extremely important and valuable piece of legislation. It introduces an important principle into arrangements for training Canada's work force and retraining people who are displaced by technological change. For this, I give the hon. gentleman all the credit I can, and all he wants. I am not sure he is right in saying this is the first time living allowances have ever been paid to trainees. I know of other places in the world where this has been done and in any case some kind of allowance was paid under the old scheme. But if the minister feels happier in making that claim, it does not worry me. The legislation is important, and I admit it. But there was no reason, other than the demands of the doctrinaire constitutional position now taken by the federal government, for scrapping every part of the old program as this measure does instead of amending the old program and making the necessary changes so that federal participation in the training of young Candians might be wider than the adult training described in this bill. The old program could have been amended and this new policy could have been grafted on to it. Obviously such a course

April 26. 1967
Occupational Training
would have interfered with the determination of the government to follow the new constitutional policy about which we shall no doubt have an opportunity to speak on other occasions.
Introduction of this legislation by regulation has meant that the minister has had to be satisfied with the consultations which took place with the provinces during formal conferences in October and November of last year. I was aware of this, and other hon. members who have spoken were aware of it. But I am sure that the minister, as a practical person who for years was an officer and later the head of an important trade union organization, knows perfectly well that this kind of legislation, which is a practical piece of work involving the daily experience of people in the field, cannot be discussed adequately at ministerial conferences. Wide-ranging discussions between representatives of this government and people concerned with adult education and training in the provinces are a matter of necessity if these provisions are to work effectively. Such consultations have obviously not taken place, to judge from press reports, and I suggest to the minister that the result of the doctrinaire position he has taken may be dangerous.
I am uneasy about the proposal in clause 3 which defines an adult as a person whose age is at least one year greater than the regular school leaving age in the province in which he resides. I know the reason for this. The minister does not want anyone to come under this plan who would normally go to a vocational training school under provincial jurisdiction, and so on. All my studies of juvenile behaviour and the incidence of juvenile delinquency have persuaded me, as others have been persuaded, that the years which are most dangerous for the juvenile are the years immediately following the day on which he ceases to attend school. This is so whether a student has dropped out because he is not interested, whether he has dropped out for economic reasons or whether he has ceased to attend for psychological, emotional or any other reasons.
In Ontario the school leaving age is 16. For a young person having left school the year which follows may well be the year in which traumatic experiences affecting the rest of his life will be encountered. Yet this period of a year must elapse before such a person is eligible for training under this scheme, even without an allowance. What can these people do in that year? All they can do is enter the unskilled labour force until they have

reached the age of 17 and are able to qualify for the training for which this bill makes provision and which is likely to be more relevant precisely because the manpower officer is given authority to relate the training given to employment possibilities.
I do not understand why the minister and his officials have introduced rigidity into the program to such a point that regardless of the situation in which an individual may find himself he cannot participate in this plan, in Ontario at least, until he is 17. The minister tries to excuse himself by saying there is a 17 year old limit in the present plan and that he has not retreated from any position previously taken. I am sure he would normally be the last to stand by something merely because it was in a former plan. It was wrong there and it is wrong here. If the minister feels he must establish a no-man's land to obviate certain difficulties which he has contemplated, I would make a suggestion to him with the best of good will and ask him to discuss it with his advisers.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I suggest it is possible to provide that the manpower officers in the department would have discretion in special circumstances to make a program available to someone immediately after leaving school. Assuming that the minister's officers are people with some humanity in them, assuming they have some experience in personnel training, job evaluation and job placement, and assuming if they have not got it now they will acquire it in time-I am not trying to needle the minister; he cannot start with personnel who are not there and there has to be a period of training -assuming these officers have the qualities which are desirable they should be given some discretion. If they have statutory discretion or discretion under the regulations they will be able to catch the unfortunate situation where the individual, in their view, deserves or requires because of special circumstances to be placed under training, without taking the risk of his either doing nothing for a year or doing something that may psychologically affect him for the rest of his working life.
I find even more objectionable the requirement that a single person without dependants must be a member of the labour force, substantially without interruption, for not less than three years. That seems to me to be an unnecessarily and heartlessly long period, unless the minister has a reason for it. What this means is that a youngster who leaves
April 26. 1967

school at age 16 or 17 cannot obtain allowances under the training plan. I appreciate that he can get training but he cannot obtain allowances under the plan until he is 19 or 20. It means that a young person who has left school at 16 or 17, or for that matter at 18, cannot obtain the allowances under this plan until he is 19, 20 or 21 and during those three years he either must enter the unskilled, untrained labour force or be available for work, without any skill, without any training, unless he can find the means from his parents, his relatives or somewhere else to enable him to enter into a training plan without receiving the allowances which this bill provides.
For the life of me I do not understand why this long period is specified. Again I suggest to the minister it is possible to do incalculable and irretrievable harm to a young man or woman during those three years. All studies of juvenile behaviour have shown that is the case, and if those three years are hopeless for the young Canadian male or female, in many cases this will do incalculable harm. Surely what we are interested in doing under this bill is to make as certain as the minister and parliament can, that young Canadians will receive opportunities to get the skills which the modern scientific age requires in order to enable them to make productive use of their labour and to make a productive contribution to the country. Perhaps the minister can give us some reasons why we need this long period of three years before a person is entitled to this; at the moment I can see none.
Despite the comments made by the minister the same is true for a married woman who suddenly becomes a widow or, even if she is not a widow, her children have grown up and she desires to go into the labour force and wants some training in order to enter the labour force. Unless I misunderstand this clause, and I do not think I do, such a woman would have to wait three years in some sort of work or be available for some sort of work before becoming entitled to the allowances provided by this bill.
Again I say that I believe it is only a doctrinaire approach to this problem which has made the minister specify three years. I do not want to speak at great length, Mr. Chairman, because I know the program that is before us today. I think I have made my point as clear as possible without repeating myself. In view of what I have said I am not going to move an amendment respecting the one year period after school leaving age because that is a little complicated, but I hope 23033-974
Occupational Training
the minister will give some thought to my suggestion about giving the manpower officers in the field some discretion so they can deal with this situation. However, Mr. Chairman, I do move the following amendment:
That clause 3(b) (i) of Bill C-273 be amended by deleting the words "three years" in line 10 thereof and substituting the words "one year" therefor.
I point out before I sit down that this amendment would bring the clause in line with the first part of the provision and would wipe out some of the defects in the clause so that if the minister insists on the one year after school leaving age remaining a general rule, a person entering the training field would be able to do so without the deprivation which many will undoubtedly suffer as a result of the three year requirement.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot but agree with the general principles outlined by the member for York South.
Naturally, I do not admit that the bill reflects a doctrinary attitude. It may reflect an attitude based on principle, but it is certainly not doctrinary.
Assuredly, it tries to set the limit between federal and provincial responsibility. Although the bill may be very specific, its scope is rather limited. Though it will have widespread results, and I feel that it is not intended to solve all the problems which may exist in the field of education and professional training of our young people or young workers.
I agree about the difficulties mentioned and the problems which will be created. I could state others. I could refer to 14 year-old children who, at a given time, have some problems and who also leave school, and this is tragic. What is done for 14 year-old children?
I am sure that the hon. member for York South is not ready to leave them aside; then, they should also be covered. This means that we must know where and when we really assume a responsibility, because if we were the only government and the only jurisdiction, I would agree with him completely, and those people would also have to be covered.
However, there is also the provincial government, and there are the municipalities, which have responsibilities, and I believe a line has to be drawn somewhere, and that is precisely what we have done.

April 26, 1967
Occupational Training
Now this does not mean that this program will forever remain as restricted as it is now. There are problems which we are considering. The member for York South himself mentioned, this morning, I believe, the quality of the personnel, the tools we need to implement such a bill, and he is right, because I find that before we venture too far in this field, without being theoretical, we must wait until we hold all the tools, well sharpened, in our hands.
Therefore, in any case, the amendment he proposes will, of course, bring about the situation I mentioned yesterday evening and this morning, which is that young people, one year after leaving school, become adults according to law and are entitled to receive an allowance.
So, he implies that he would not touch the first part, but nevertheless he touches it by touching the second, because by bringing back the definition of an adult and tying it down to a year in the labour force, this means that the youngster coming out of school and waiting for one year or working for one year is eligible for allowances at that time, and the effect is exactly the same.
So, I do not know-he understood my position on the first point, he does not seem to understand it on the second, although exactly the same situation is repeated.
Anyway, I believe this will upset the entire financial set-up of this legislation. I think the reasons given have no sense, and I do not believe that we could, at this stage, accept an amendment of this type and run the risk of severely upsetting our school system.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
which it seems to me the federal government has an obligation to give. This is the reason I simply cannot accept the explanation the minister has given for his opposition to the amendment.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say just a few words. Of course, if the hon. member does not recognize that there is a constitution in Canada or if he believes that we should not care about it-
Oh, oh.
Well, there is a constitution and it means something.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. The minister has received from me, my colleagues and many other hon. members the courtesy of accepting his sincerity. Now he makes the kind of statement which turns me either into a moron or into something even worse. Whatever else I may be, I am not this. I know there is a constitution in Canada. I know there are divisions of power. I realize as surely as the minister does the difficulties which there are in any federal state. Those difficulties, however, are not solved by building walls such as those which divide East and West Berlin.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Chairman, I have no intention whatever of insulting the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis). Obviously, if a constitutional problem is involved, concepts may be quite different over the way Canada should operate and I do not see why I should be a depository of eternal truth and he should be mistaken, or vice versa.
So, I am not at all at that level, but as far as we are concerned we take the attitude that, in the field of education, the provinces have jurisdiction and should exert it.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Otherwise, we will always be faced with problems. It may be that our philosophy is wrong; in that case, we shall have to decide at the political level with the people involved, how the Canadian people conceive this country. This problem may be over my head, as well as that of some of my colleagues in this house, but the Canadian people will determine in what kind of a country we shall live.
As far as we are concerned, we believe that when a provincial jurisdiction is clearly established, the province should deal with it 23033-974J
Occupational Training
and we naturally should help, if possible. This is what we are doing. When the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) says: You have withdrawn from vocational training, thus depriving Nova Scotia of the necessary equipment and institutions, I must tell him for his information that I have mentioned several times that we have not withdrawn from this program; on the contrary, we have extended the provisions of capital investments in the area of vocational training. As far as cost is concerned, we are ready to pay not only the cost of operation and administration, but also part of the depreciation of invested capital, so that the province may be in a position to build schools and to equip them properly.
In addition, we are ready to lend money to the provinces to enable them to be adequately equipped for vocational training.
I cannot understand how the hon. member for York South can say that we have withdrawn from this field telling the provinces: You handle this responsibility by yourselves while, in fact, under this new program, we are doing more than we were doing before.
Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the concept will be settled outside the house, but I also believe that the House of Commons must leave provincial responsibilities with provincial legislatures. If the provinces have a responsibility in the field of juvenile delinquency, they must handle that; on the other hand, if they cannot assume their responsibilities, they can negotiate with the federal government, but it is not for us to get further into areas of provincial jurisdiction.

Mr. Chairman, I believe the debate which has been going on for a while between the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) and the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) is a very good illustration of what I have always thought, namely that the constitution gives powers and jurisdictions to both the federal and provincial levels of government.
Mr. Chairman, we are precisely witnessing an effort to initiate an occupational training plan by a federal government which, because of certain jurisdictional limitations, keeps saying: We cannot do this, we cannot do that, because education comes under provincial jurisdiction.
The hon. member for York South is putting forward an argument which should be supported, in an attempt to have the three-year period, during which an adult should have

April 26, 1967
Occupational Training
played a part in the labour market or have been a member of the labour force, reduced to one year.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration rises and says: I agree with the objectives mentioned by the hon. member for York South, it is good common sense, I would accept all that, but unfortunately, it cannot be done, because it is another government that has jurisdiction in the educational field. The legislation actually cannot achieve the objective that would be the most advisable and the most desirable, since there are precisely two different jurisdictions. The federal government appropriates certain jurisdictions, recognizes other provincial jurisdictions and the provincial government also has jurisdictions. Therefore, what will the legislation be?
Mr. Chairman, it is going to be precisely what the Minister of Manpower and Immigration stated, and it is going to be what the hon. member for York South would not want it to be, namely a compromise, precisely because there are two jurisdictions, and there will be nine provinces, driving at centralization, that are going to bear the consequences and the after-effects thereof. Nine provinces would like centralization in the field of occupational training and education and will not get it. Why? Because one province is against it and says: Education is our responsibility; it falls under our jurisdiction. The constitution grants us that, so we want to keep our autonomy in the field of education.
The federal government will reach a solution which, in the end, will only be a compromise and will have to take into account some constitutional acts, some jurisdictions, in short some touchy people. That compromise will only endanger the success of a piece of legislation which could reach its objective but will not reach it precisely because it is based on a compromise. As a matter of fact, that is how Canada has been forging ahead from one compromise to another since 1867.
Two trends have been clearly set forth this afternoon in the house. Nine provinces tend as much as possible toward centralization in certain fields, whereas Quebec is tending towards autonomy. There is a clash between the two trends which results in endless compromises and half-measures and, as the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) rightly said earlier, the piece of legislation we will pass today will only be a half-measure, precisely because of the two different trends.

They are opposed and harmful to each other; they cannot exist together and when they are made to do so, they are prejudicial to the full implementation of comprehensive pieces of legislation, either in the field of occupational training or in other fields.
Yesterday, Mr. Chairman, I proposed an amendment on this very matter in order to satisfy both aspirations and avoid the passing of half-measures.
If Quebec could opt out of this legislation and get fiscal compensation in return, the federal government could then legislate for the other nine provinces. But the latter would be ready and willing to give Ottawa as much jurisdiction as possible in this connection, and Ottawa would then be able to pass a much more complete legislation than the present one, because the other provinces would not be opposed to federal intervention in matters under provincial jurisdiction.
For its part, Quebec would get financial compensation, the funds necessary to enable it to administer this same act. The province could administer the act entirely, providing even greater help for those who are to benefit by this legislation. The two groups would be pleased and both aspirations would be satisfied-that of the province of Quebec towards autonomy and that of the nine other provinces toward centralization. The legislation could then be improved, in Quebec as well as in the nine other provinces, for Quebec alone would be in charge of the implementation of this legislation and, therefore, there would be no conflict of jurisdiction such as the one we are witnessing now.
This conflict was admitted by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration himself when he said: If there were no provincial jurisdiction in the field of education, I would agree with the remarks of the hon. member for York South, because we would then be the only government and the only jurisdiction involved.
Mr. Chairman, it is precisely there that something does not work. There are two different tendencies and they would like to compound both. Instead of leaving each one to its own, they try to check them. Quebec should be left free in its tendency towards autonomy and given fiscal equivalence which would give the province sources of income equivalent to what the federal government would spend. Then the Quebec tendency towards autonomy would be respected, and the other nine provinces would-

Mr. Chairman, very briefly I would like to indicate why I and my colleagues, I believe, will support the amendment presented by the hon. member for York South. To save repetition I will make my argument by quoting two paragraphs from page 172 of the first annual review of the Economic Council of Canada which I think put the matter in very good perspective. They read as follows:
There are three major kinds of labour mobility: occupational, industrial and geographical. An unemployed worker may face the need to undergo one, or two, or all three. In some cases, a worker may become displaced because his skill has become obsolete, and cannot be transferred elsewhere.
May I add that this could happen even to a person with only one year of employment in a particular industry.
To be re-absorbed into the labour market, he will have to acquire a new skill. This means retraining. In other cases, a displaced worker may be the victim of a declining industry.
Again this could happen to a person employed for only one year in a particular industry.
This may or may not require his learning a new skill, depending on whether or not his present skill is transferable. If he lives in a community where there are no alternatives, he will have no choice but to move to a new locality if he is to find employment.
The importance of labour mobility has increased in recent years-
I suggest this is a very substantial part of the problem of labour mobility.
-largely as a result of an acceleration in technological change and a more closely interdependent international economy. Occupational skills can be quickly wiped out through a new technical process.
Again this can happen to a person who has been in a job for only one year. Why should he be required to wait two more years

April 26, 1967

before some help is given him? I continue to quote.
Whole industries can be sent into decline, either from technological advancements, from increasing import competition, or from changes in consumer demand.
We know how rapidly change can occur in that field.
The day is probably gone when a new entrant into the labour force could reasonably expect to make one skill last throughout his working life, or, perhaps, to stay permanently in the same occupation, industry or locality.
These are words of great common sense. If a person, particularly a young person just entering the labour market who has had to put certain amounts of money into furniture, a home, a car and the like, loses his employment and we cannot give him immediate and fast relief, then we are not fulfilling our responsibility. For this reason the official opposition will support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for York South.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (for the Minister of Finance) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE FIVE PER CENT REFUNDABLE TAX
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-280, to amend the Income Tax Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) gave the house notice of his intention to introduce this bill at the close of business on March 10 last. Because it is provided in the bill that it take effect from March 31, 1967, he had hoped that parliament would be able to deal with it before that date. However, as hon. members know, the parliamentary timetable made this impossible.
The purpose of the bill is to terminate, effective March 31, the tax period to which the special 5 per cent refundable tax on business profits applies and also to terminate on the same date the period of collection of the tax from corporations. In the case of trusts which are subject to the tax, payments may need to be made in June or September, but the over-all liability will be reduced in the same way as for corporations. Corporations may have to make some adjusting payment after March where their monthly instalments have not amounted to the precise amount of the tax as and when it is determined. This means that payments of that tax for April 1967 will not be required.
It will be recalled that this refundable tax was imposed as a special temporary measure to divert and immobilize temporarily a modest portion of the flows of funds that are the chief sources of finance for capital expenditures of businesses. It has applied to all corporations that are liable for income tax and to those trusts that have income from a business or from rentals. It was made effective for an 18-month period from May 1, 1966 to October 31, 1967 and was made payable for corporations in monthly instalments starting on May 31 last.
The tax was imposed on a special base which was devised to approximate the cash flow of a corporation. For example, in addition to taxable income as computed for income tax purposes this base included the
April 26, 1967

amount of capital cost allowances and depletion allowances deducted in computing income. On the other hand, the base was reduced by amounts paid as income taxes and by amounts paid in repayment of long-term debt.
This short Bill C-280 is quite simple. It merely substitutes the words "March 31, 1967" for the words "October 31, 1967" where they appear in the present law. This will apply to the definition of the tax period, which will reduce the total liability for the tax to a corresponding degree. It will also apply to the dates on which payments of tax have to be made.
No change is proposed at this time in the provisions for repaying the tax. The law will continue to provide that the tax shall be refunded, with interest at the rate of 5 per cent, at such time or times as the governor in council may prescribe by regulation, but that in any case this time shall not be less than 18 months or more than 36 months after the date on which the instalment was due, or the date on which it was paid if that is later.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
My main remarks today relate to the reasons for proposing this bill. They apply, too, to an associated measure, which had the same purpose as this bill, on which action was taken by the government last month. This measure was the provision in the Income Tax Act regulations under which capital assets of certain classes acquired in the period after the date of the March 1966 budget but before October 1 of this year would be subject to deferred capital cost allowances. On March 22 last the Minister of Finance tabled order in council P.C. 1967-533 of March 21, which changed from October 1 to April 1 of this year the date at which this period was to come to an end.
It will be recalled that when the minister brought down the budget for 1966-67 on March 29 last year he reported the Canadian economy was under a good deal of strain. Most sectors and regions of the economy were working to full capacity and shortages of skilled labour had become evident. The pace of economic expansion was such indeed that unless some of the demands for goods and services and labour and other resources were moderated and postponed, the pressure upon prices and wages would become inflationary and there would be danger that the boom would culminate in an economic recession.
As a consequence of the conditions at the time, the Minister of Finance proposed a
Income Tax Act
number of measures designed to pace and to prolong the prosperity. Among these were two measures of a temporary nature designed to moderate the rate of increase in the capital expenditures of business and to stretch it out over a longer period. This included the refundable tax on the cash profits of corporations and certain trusts, the subject matter of the bill before the house, and a deferral of a portion of the capital cost allowances which could be claimed on assets acquired after the budget date. In explaining the purpose and advantages of these measures, he mentioned that each could be terminated on short notice without serious effects, should our economic circumstances change substantially. This was in accordance with the general policy he had stated in that budget of keeping our fiscal policies flexible and readily adaptable to changing circumstances.
During the months following the budget the necessity for restraint in the economy became even more evident than it had been earlier. The activity and market effects of the excessive economic demands helped to produce excessive price and wage pressures of dangerous proportions. Some moderation of these demands was evident during the summer months but was not sufficient to accomplish what was necessary in regard to the increases in prices and costs.
On September 8, therefore, the Minister of Finance made a major statement in the House of Commons in which he outlined certain decisions the government had taken in order
to further dampen the inflationary pressures on the economy. These related chiefly to government expenditures. He also called upon all Canadians to moderate their demands on the economy. Hon. members will recall the rather forceful public debates to which these measures gave rise, particularly of course the deferment of certain government programs.
The last three months of 1966 and the early months of this year have been moderation in the rate of increase in demands on the Canadian economy. It appeared by December that the rate of expansion had moderated to a much more sustainable level. Consequently the supplementary budget of December 19, introduced for the purpose of financing the guaranteed income supplement for old age security pensions, was essentially a neutral budget. My colleague the Minister of Finance said at the time that the economy seemed to be in a state of delicate balance and that our economic policies should be designed then neither to stimulate nor to restrain economic activity. He stated that should the economy

April 26, 1967
Incovie Tax Act
show signs of weakness we would be prepared to act quickly to relax the temporary fiscal restraints of the March budget.
I do not wish today to anticipate the budget he will be bringing down next month, nor the white paper on the Canadian economy which will accompany it. However, I will refer briefly to the events in 1967 which led the Minister of Finance to terminate the temporary measure introduced in the March 1966 budget. During the early months of the year the more moderate rate of growth of the economy continued. When my colleague introduced this bill in March, and when the government acted on the deferred capital cost allowances, it seemed evident that the rate of expansion this year would likely be considerably less than last year and within our potential capacity, taking into account the growth of the labour force and the increased industrial capacity acquired in recent years. Consequently he said that restraints upon capital expenditures seemed no longer to be required. The slower rate of growth in capital expenditures was subsequently shown in detail in the survey of private and public investment intentions, undertaken jointly by the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. It showed that planned investment spending in Canada in 1967 would increase only moderately over
1966	investment expenditures, in contrast with the large increases in 1966 over 1965.
We were also influenced in our decision by the signs of moderation in the rate of increase of United States economic activity. In particular, the survey of the intentions of American business in regard to its investment plans for 1967, conducted by the department of commerce and the securities and exchange commission, showed an increase much less for
1967	than for last year. It was not clear what was likely to happen to the rate of economic expansion in the United States in the latter half of the year, but it seemed fairly evident that during the first half there would be some slowing down. It will be recalled that President Johnson had recommended to Congress reinstatement of the 7 per cent investment credit that was suspended late last year and the accelerated rates of capital cost allowances which had also been suspended.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
The action that has been taken in regard to capital cost allowances, and that which is provided for in this bill in regard to the refundable tax will encourage businesses in

Canada to proceed with plans for capital expenditures this year and next year at more normal rates than would have been likely had these temporary restrictions remained. The 5 per cent refundable tax on business profits has been bringing in something of the order of $18 million a month from businesses to the government, which we have been deliberately holding idle in our cash balances, as he indicated was our intention last March. This flow of cash from business to the government has now ceased. We will feel free to utilize temporarily the funds that we have accumulated since last May. This will give us more flexibility in our demands upon the capital market during this coming fiscal year, although there is every indication that these demands will be high in any case, taking into account the high level of our expenditures and the very large amounts that we are lending, particularly through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for housing and urban development and also through the Farm Credit Corporation for farm purposes.
We have not proposed in this bill any change in the provisions of the law concerning the dates of repayment of the refundable tax. This is a matter which I believe should more appropriately be considered during the preparation of the 1967 budget.
The resumption of normal rates of capital cost allowances in April will have an effect upon our revenues this fiscal year. It is difficult to estimate these with precision at this time, but our advisers tell us that the action will probably reduce the income tax revenue by about $60 million compared with what it would have been had the original termination date of September 30 been left in the regulations.
In addition to this effect on our revenues, there will be some additional effect in the reduction of accruing tax obligations of businesses, which should have some influence on their behaviour.
It is our hope that the action provided for in this measure and that taken in regard to capital cost allowances, along with whatever action we may propose in the budget, will enable us to maintain high levels of employment, production and income while keeping the increases in prices and costs this year down to more modest and tolerable levels.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE FIVE PER CENT REFUNDABLE TAX
speechtext:
I welcome the new Minister without Portfolio in his first appearance in his new role, and wish him success. I regret, however, that the present and the former ministers of finance are not with us this afternoon.
As the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) has said, this measure reveals the hit or miss ad hoc fiscal politics of this government. I think this bill can hardly be discussed without considering another fiscal policy introduced by the former minister of finance; the attitudes displayed in these two pieces of policy are revealing.
As you may recall, Mr. Speaker, the former minister of finance instituted a tax cut on personal income which, at the time it was introduced, I criticized on the grounds that it was clumsy and unimaginative. That measure provided tax relief for many taxpayers who did not really need it and who should not have been afforded it, and it gave no real relief to those in the lower income brackets. I was interested to find that the former minister of finance apparently had never heard of the concept of tax credits, which might have solved his problem without the necessity of granting tax relief to those who did not need it.
Our present Minister of Finance has repealed that particular measure which was designed inadequately and clumsily to benefit some individual taxpayers, and now he proposes to repeal a tax placed on another sector
of the economy represented by the business interests of Canada.
When this measure was introduced I felt impelled to criticize it for its ineptitude and failure to follow any definite principle. I suggested that the Minister of Finance might with advantage read an article on the fiscal policies of the Swedish government. That government's policies with respect to refundable taxes is that they are funds which are neutralized until the government decides it is wise to release them into investment again. This measure, on the other hand, does not neutralize funds obtained from such tax, because 5 per cent interest, coming from the taxpayers of Canada, is paid on the amount gathered. The measure also ties the minister's hands.
Regardless of the developments taking place in the country, the minister applied the tax for a certain period, after which he would release the funds. Regardless of whether the economy improved or did not improve, stayed the same or did not stay the same, the amount so collected was collected for a definite period. This struck me, at the time, as an example of how this government has repeatedly acted. It makes a gesture which appears to aim in one direction and then it nullifies that gesture by a subsequent action.
As a means of controlling the economy it was obvious that the 5 per cent refundable tax, under the terms in which it was passed by this house, was useless. First, it was too small in scale; second, the minister, as I have said, had no freedom of action to use the funds derived from this type of tax in such a way as to control the economy, to stimulate it, or to curb it where it was necessary to curb it.

I doubt if the measure had any serious impact. It may have had a slight impact.
What has happened is a revelation of the different attitudes this government has toward the individual taxpayer, particularly the one in the lower income bracket, and the business world. That difference in attitude is exhibited in this measure.
The government is to remove the tax affecting business; I heard no suggestion of restoring the 10 per cent tax cut on personal

April 26, 1967
Income Tax Act
income tax. Perhaps that is because the present minister realizes that his predecessor in the area of this measure was somewhat inept and clumsy. I should have thought that the minister would have had access to more sophisticated thinking, and that he might have considered tax credits to overcome the problem of granting tax relief to those who do not require it. He did neither of these things. In the light of the public's attitude toward the Government of Canada-and that attitude is important whether one supports the government or not-I think the minister has been unwise. He has been unwise to reveal so clearly that this government is interested primarily in the business community and not in the ordinary citizen.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
The minister might have achieved the same result-the result contemplated in this measure-by the reinstatement in a sophisticated way of the 10 per cent tax cut with respect to personal incomes. He chose, instead of doing that, to place a time limit on the imposition of the 5 per cent refundable tax. We can be thankful that the other taxpayers of Canada will no longer need to pay 5 per cent interest on this refundable tax, a tax which amounted to a forced investment on the part of business in government at a certain interest rate; part of the profits had to be turned over to the government.
The present Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) should look at some of the speeches he made when members of this side of the house put it to him that he should be considering our fiscal policies in a much more comprehensive way than he has done so far. I recall several occasions upon which 1 was told I could not expect any comprehensive survey of our fiscal policies until the Carter report had been tabled. Curiously enough the only people who have said anything about the Carter report are members of this group in the House of Commons-perhaps representatives of the official opposition have made some comment on it-and the business community which, of course, has been squealing to high heaven. As far as the government is concerned the report has been received with a blank silence-not one word about it, except that it will not be implemented now.
The Minister without Portfolio might well suggest to his colleague the Minister of Finance that before he continues these ad hoc measures, changing one part of our fiscal policy here and another there, he should examine the Carter report to see whether we cannot

put our fiscal policies into a more coherent framework in order that individual taxpayers as well as the business community may have a clearer idea of what lies before them. If this were done the people of Canada would also be in a better position to judge what is the political and economic philosophy of this government when it comes to a choice between the various sectors of our economy.
I suggest to the Minister without Portfolio that by the repeal of this 5 per cent refundable tax his government is revealing itself as one which is firmly wedded to the interests of the business community. This is part of the doctrinaire approach about which I and others have complained freely of late-a concept that the purpose of government is to serve the interests of those who conduct the businesses of Canada. It is a concept which implies at least that the most important section of our community consists not of ordinary citizens in their capacity as consumers, workers and salary-earners but of those who are in the position of being able to profit by the operations of business.
The proposal before us does at least reveal the position of the government. But I would seriously recommend to the Minister of Finance that he begin to evolve a coherent economic and political philosophy and put an end to this hit or miss approach-this making of empty gestures in an attempt to convince the people of Canada that he has some coherent policy and is concerned about the welfare of the whole of the community. He will not achieve this object by the sudden removal of the refundable tax, with all its shortcomings and limitations when at the same time he does nothing whatever to restore the 10 per cent personal income tax cut which was allowed by his predecessor.

A few words in connection with the short bill which is before us. I do not think there was any doubt in the minister's mind that this refundable tax was something of an experiment. I am pleased to see the tax is being removed.
I find myself both agreeing and disagreeing with what was said by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron). We believe more emphasis should be placed on the ability of taxpayers generally to meet their obligations. I know that the business community to which the hon. member referred is highly

aware of the fact that little business is possible if people do not have money in their pockets to spend. Thus the business community is very much interested in the distribution of purchasing power in this country.
I do not think it is correct to suggest that we must take the side of business or else take the side of the individual taxpayer. The whole process of production and consumption must be considered as a totality; it cannot be divided into parts. No matter how it is organized the business community must provide the necessities of life to the individual. The better we organize ourselves and take advantage of cybernation, the more our standard of living will rise.
I am concerned that the government and the Minister of Finance have not as yet found a way of looking after those regions where there is special need for capital expansion. I realize that this may present difficulties when at the same time inflationary pressures are building up in other parts of the nation-
