speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the people of this great nation of ours are very fortunate indeed that there are provisions in our parliamentary rules which make it possible from time to time in this particular debate to bring to the attention of the government grievances from those segments of the population which feel they are not receiving the treatment to which they are duly entitled or, on the other hand, bring to the attention of the government, on behalf of a segment of the Canadian population, a policy laid down by the government which seems to be placing a direct and dire hardship on that particular segment. It is in respect of the latter that I wish to speak tonight.
Mr. Chairman, you will recall that some two weeks ago an attempt was made to set aside the regular business of this house in order to promote with the government a debate on the plight of the entire dairy industry in Canada today. You will recall that parliament in its wisdom refused this debate on this
April 26, 1967

particular occasion, indicating that we would have a later opportunity to discuss this important matter. We on this side of the house felt that there was a great deal of merit in calling for the emergency debate, because it was our considered opinion that the government's new dairy policy which had been in operation for only a few weeks was creating chaos in the dairy industry and was bringing about a direct hardship rather than a benefit.
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
Our feelings were borne out by the fact that wherever in this nation the dairy industry formed a great part of the economy, emergency meetings were held. At these meetings the dairy farmers expressed the feeling that this new policy would not suffice to meet their critical needs. Indeed there were and still are rumours about a parade of dairy farmers in the thousands to parliament hill to protest this policy. There also have been rumours that it might be necessary for these farmers to promote a strike similar to that which was held in the United States, including the dumping of precious dairy supplies on the ground and the selling of dairy cattle. This would cause a disruption which would be felt right through the economy to the consumer level.
It is our hope tonight that by bringing these problems to the attention of the government some measures will be adopted which will make such contemplated action in this country unnecessary. Surely it would be to no one's benefit to have food destroyed at this time when it is so precious to the peoples of this world.
This government took great credit for the proposals set out to the dairy industry when this new policy was introduced. Whether the government intended it or not at that time, it left the impression with opposition members in this house and with members of the Canadian agricultural industry as a whole that in its opinion the farmers had never had things so good. When the Minister of Agriculture announced the new policy he indicated, and I believe rightly so, that while this government had been in office the price per hundredweight of manufactured milk, based on a 3.5 test, had increased from $2.85 to $4.75. He seemed to take undue satisfaction from the fact that what this government had accomplished had been more than that accomplished by the previous government.
Let us examine the figures for a moment to see what has happened to the dairy industry.
Interim Supply
The $2.85 per hundredweight is presumably what the producers of milk actually received during the fiscal year prior to 1962-63, and the $4.75 per hundredweight is the amount the minister alleges will be paid to the producers this year. In the first place these figures are not accurate. The farmers will not receive $4.75 per hundredweight because, as it was indicated earlier, 10 to 11 cents per hundredweight will be required to finance the export of excess dairy products. In addition to that we must consider the 12 per cent sales tax which farmers must pay, the increase in old age pension tax, the contribution to the Canada Pension Fund-which in itself is a tax-the increase in income tax, the drastic increase in the cost of living and the tremendous increase in the cost of goods and services which the farmer must have in order to produce milk.
It is astonishing to find, after analysing the situation, that farmers in 1962 receiving $2.85 per hundredweight actually netted more than they will today under the new dairy policy. That may be astonishing but it is the economic fact. When we refer to the fact that producers of fluid milk are in dire circumstances due to the withdrawal of federal subsidies- and I want to be fair-I am sure members of the government will indicate that this is a matter of provincial concern.
These salient points are so important that some of my colleagues who will follow me intend to deal in greater detail with the causes of the direct hardships dairy farmers are now experiencing. In my view the dairy farmers have every right to parade to parliament hill to protest. If I thought it would add anything to their cause I would join them in this parade. We have learned from experience that representations to this government have little or no result so far as relief is concerned.
When these farmers come to parliament hill they can only once again present the facts and proposals which they have already presented. I might add, these representations were made to this government before this new policy was determined or announced. Certainly their problems are not new, but it is unfortunate that this government since it took office has never put into effect one single recommendation proposed by the various representatives of the agricultural industry. These representatives are directly concerned with this great industry and have every right to approach the federal government in respect of their problems. The plight in which they find themselves today is a direct result of the

April 26, 1967
Interim Supply
course of action of federal governments over the past years. These governments have interfered directly with the operation of this industry by establishing additional payments, bonuses, stabilization activities and subsidies. It is no wonder this great industry is out of balance from time to time.
Representatives of this industry proposed the formation of a national dairy commission which could deal with the industry's problems, so that permanent solutions could be found and concrete things done on their behalf. I believe this is a sound proposal. Apparently the government adopted the proposal, and in this regard we supported the government. But what happened? We find now that the government is in process of going in the opposite direction. The first thing it did under the new policy was to put the producers of fluid milk and producers of manufactured milk in different categories. This government cut the industry in half by putting one part under provincial jurisdiction and the other part under federal jurisdiction. We now have a national dairy council which can only concern itself with one half of the industry.
This government went a step further. We now have three segments of government looking after national dairy interests. We have the National Dairy Council, the stabilization board and the Department of Agriculture. I suspect that like many of the commissions set up by the government, the National Dairy Council, with all its good intentions and with its high calibre of men, will be hamstrung by direct interference from the other two levels of government.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
So we find that the dairy industry is now in chaos, it is in confusion and there seems to be no direct policy in this regard. As I said before, the government took great pride in the introduction of this dairy policy for the coming year. We used to believe that this government had no policy for agriculture, but this has proved to be not the case as far as the dairy industry is concerned, for here the reverse is true; this government has been in office for four years and we have had four distinct and separate dairy policies, one for each year. We ask therefore why will the government not listen to the recommendations of the industry and promote a policy for the welfare of the industry rather than for political expediency?
The Minister of Agriculture in his very capable way in the house, on the hustings, on radio and television has put forward the proposition that millions of dollars are being

poured into the dairy industry in the form of direct subsidies. He has said that the price obtained by the producers of manufactured milk is higher than it has ever been in the history of this country. The minister says that all is well in the industry, dairy production is as high as it has ever been and the returns are greater on a dollar basis than they have ever been.
Let us deal with these various assertions. First of all, with regard to the millions of dollars being poured into the dairy industry in the form of direct subsidies, if you look at the records of the stabilization board and the Department of Agriculture with regard to the payments made to the dairy industry-and I am speaking of net cost to the government-a startling picture becomes apparent. It seems that as far as dairy farmers are concerned the policy of this government is progressively to reduce the amount of stabilization funds, and not increase them. We find that whereas in 1963 farmers in the dairy industry received $117 million in subsidies, the figure was reduced to $55 million last year. This is a reduction of $62 million.
I point out to the committee that this industry is marginal and is struggling to maintain itself. The government tells us that the dairy industry never had it so good. This is the impression they wish to leave across the country. What about the status of the industry today? Dairy production is as high as it has ever been. However, this situation reflects absolutely no credit on the government; the credit is due to the men and women who look after the dairy herds. The average dairy farm production has risen to such a degree that it is maintaining the industry in Canada. But production has almost reached its ultimate. I believe that in the future we will see a drastic curtailment in dairy production unless action is taken now to halt the chaos that exists in the industry. As a matter of fact, the production of milk today has been kept on a par with previous years, although in the last four years there has been a reduction in top-notch dairy cattle and young stock of almost 600,000 animals. These are the best animals we have in Canada.
It is a sad sight indeed to visit the export ports of this country and see these fine animals with their excellent pedigrees, these foundation stock animals, being exported all over the world. Only two parties can profit from this type of action, the merchants concerned in the purchase and sale of the cattle and those in the foreign country who purchase the animals knowing their value. It is a
April 26, 1967

sad day when we see this decimation of our very best herds. This decimation is taking place at an alarming rate and I believe the figures published are in keeping with the actual fact. In my county alone, which at one time was a top producer of dairy products, I was very alarmed to find out from the Department of Agriculture a few weeks ago that the number of producers of milk, which was 18 to 35 on each of many routes, has dropped to only 72 in the entire county. This is the number of milk producers left in a county of
90.000	people.
It is said that we have never had it so good. Whenever we criticize the government they always come back with those two shop-worn phrases, namely what did you do when you were in office, and, are you against our present policy? As an indication of what we did while in office-and we were in office for only six years-I would point out that at that time the dairy products of this country were in excess. As a matter of fact, the main problem confronting the Department of Agriculture at that time was the storage of excess dairy products. It may be said that this government has depleted these stocks by supersalesmanship. This is not true. The stock of 200 million to 300 million pounds of butter was decimated by a fire sale in order to balance the government's budget for the 1965 election. This is what happened to the tremendous carry-over of dairy stocks; and now we are importing the very products which we gave away.
Hon. members opposite try to criticize us, but the record speaks for itself. They find it impossible to refute the fact that there are far fewer creameries in Canada today than there were just four years ago; there are fewer dairies in Canada today than there were four years ago; there are far fewer farmers in the dairy industry in Canada today than there were four years ago. To give the committee an indication of the reduction in the number of labourers on the farms today I would point out that with respect to a bill that was before the house a few hours ago, that concerned with the retraining of workers, it was said that provision may have to be made to retrain
500.000	labourers who are leaving the farms. This is the problem with which we are faced today. There is only one way to describe the condition of the dairy industry; that is, that there exists confusion and chaos through no fault of those in the industry.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
We feel it is time that this government started to formulate policies which will save
Interim Supply
the major industries of this country. The dairy industry today would not be able to support itself were it not for the tremendous immigration into this country in the past few years of top flight dairy farmers from the Netherlands, Denmark and from other countries. I have nothing but words of praise for the great effort put forth by these men, who are promoting the dairy industry against almost impossible odds.
I come back to the fact that the dairy industry is in trouble. Farmers would not be taking time off from their busy lives to go to meetings, they would not be promoting demonstrations for no good reason. They are fine, sound, educated businessmen, because a man who wants to stay in the farming industry today must be a businessman. When these businessmen take the time off to approach parliament hill it is because they feel the situation is critical. Therefore my request to the government tonight is to call in the leaders of the dairy industry, not just the few known party supporters but the men who are generally concerned with the industry and the future of the Canadian population. The government should listen to their representations and not just give them a polite hearing. It should analyse their propositions. These men are businessmen who have advanced these propositions only after thoroughly scrutinizing their feasibility and the ways and means to help this great industry. If they receive a sympathetic hearing from the Department of Agriculture, if new ways are determined to bring direct financial relief, and if the government brings the dairy industry under one jurisdiction instead of dividing the responsibility, thereby relieving itself of all direct criticism-which might be politically expedient but which does not solve anything-then we would consider this to be a step forward.
I think the time has long passed when this last mentioned method of dealing with the basic Canadian industry can be used. The government has announced a dairy policy but it has indicated that a year is needed to assess it properly. A year in the dairy industry will see a great number of remaining farms close down. It is not only the small farms that will be affected but also farms that are milking anywhere from 60 to 150 cattle, farms which, using the best businesslike approach, find it impossible to continue under the present circumstances.
This is not just a problem which faces the farmer and the primary producer. It faces also the manufacturer and the distributor.

April 26. 1967
Interim Supply
Now is the time When we should consider all aspects of the industry, so that all the cards can be placed on the table and a feasible method determined whereby each section of the industry will be able to continue to operate at a reasonable profit. This does not seem possible under the present government policy. The announcement of four policies in four years can only mean that the government has no basic policy and that it is experimenting at the cost of the industry.
The dairy industry of Canada has been patient far too long. It will not show sympathy for this government's experiments which are costly in men, in cattle and in our over-all production. If our immigration policies are sound in the next few years we will be faced with a tremendous influx of population. We will be faced with great expansion in the industry, if the economic climate is one quarter as good as is indicated by government spokesmen. If this takes place, there will be a great expansion in the dairy industry in order to provide the Canadian people with basic requirements in dairy products. Now is the time to take action, not a year from now. We cannot brook any further delay. The opposition in parliament is determined to see that the government is not allowed to forget this problem which is facing us.

speechtext: I understand the hon. member for Yorkton has a question for the Minister of Agriculture.

Mr. Chairman, I do not really like to contradict one of my confreres, but can he tell me why several years ago milk for the children in the schools in Ottawa was replaced by orange juice? Let us be logical. Milk comes from Canada and orange juice comes from Florida. So every Friday I give my children some milk for their ten o'clock recess.
Speak to the point.
Mr. Chairman, this is relevant. I pay my taxes yet I have to give my children 55 cents every Monday for orange juice.
Why does the hon member not speak French?

I will be bilingual, but if the hon. member wants to hear it, it will not be a compliment. Recently we have been fighting for a dairy policy. We want a branch of the department for our farmers and we want milk, butter and cream for our people. However, when a big area, such as the greater

Ottawa valley, switches from milk to orange juice, there can be no explanation. Their excuse for doing it is that milk at ten o'clock in the morning destroys the children's appetite for the noon meal. Let hon. members fight that one out.

Not long ago I was asked by a farmer who represented the farmers on one of the provincial boards which was investigating the price of farm machinery whether I was not of the opinion that it was really too late for farmers to do anything about their particular problem because they had lost so many members that they ceased to be an effective pressure group. He asked me whether it was not a fact that as the number of farmers dwindled, their problem would receive less and less attention. I am of the opinion that this is not the case. I believe that although the farming community is decreasing because many of their members have left the rural areas of Canada to join the industrial segment of our economy, they are not doing so by choice. They are there because of economic conditions which force them to be there. In my opinion the children who have been raised on farms, with no opportunity to enter this industry, are bound to come to the conclusion that something must be done to develop an economic agricultural climate in this industry, and the government should learn this before it is too late.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
We listened this afternoon to another debate in which we were discussing the retraining of workers and at that time the question of the constitution was raised. I think we in this house are plagued with the raising of constitutional points of view on the part of one or two provinces which really have little basis in fact, and in any event have no basis of popular support.
We in Ontario were very proud of the operation which took place a year ago in the province of Quebec where that province gave a much larger grant to their manufactured milk producers than was the case in Ontario. The minister got himself into the middle of this particular constitutional problem. The minister of agriculture of Ontario, Mr. Stewart, said that this was Ottawa's problem, whereas our Minister of Agriculture said it was a provincial problem and he would not get involved in it.
A solution to the problem occurred last year with the promise of the minister to take up the 25 cents that was being paid in Quebec at
April 26, 1967

the time if the province of Ontario would pay the 25 cents on a temporary basis. We now have an arrangement whereby the federal government has decided to get into the manufactured milk field, and yet under the constitution can claim that fluid milk is not a matter that falls within their jurisdiction.
I am sure that many hon. members are confused about this matter. There are many farmers in the country confused over the problem of jurisdiction in this field. But surprising as it may be, Mr. Chairman, the federal government has decided it will enter the relatively uncontrolled field of secondary milk production for manufacturing purposes, at the same time leaving the fluid milk in the hands of the provinces.
Most provincial acts which govern the marketing of fluid milk originated in the province of British Columbia. I am not aware of the extent of the British Columbia legislation, except to the extent that it has been applied in other provinces. However, I think we should take a very close look at some of the problems which are going to develop out of the arrangements which have been made, and it may therefore be wise to consider what these arrangements are.
I have had considerable knowledge over many years of the fluid milk market. For a number of years my father was an executive officer of the Ontario fluid milk producers. He was a member of a number of agencies concerned with the development of fluid milk marketing legislation and over the years acquired some knowledge of this particular field.
Farmers producing fluid milk built up an industry that was considerably larger than manufactured milk operations. They were under strict control as to the type of milk they produced. All of their farms were inspected. The milk board established, through a co-operative arrangement with the producers and the marketing agency, quotas which imposed upon the producers many responsibilities, including supplying the quantity of milk that the quota called for.
As a result, Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member for Kent (Ont.) pointed out, there were built up not only in Ontario but in other provinces as well some very high grade dairy units. These fluid milk producers bred herds which have since been exported to places such as Guyana, France and Great Britain. In fact, our cattle, particularly our dairy breeds, have been exported to many countries in the world, with much credit to the producers.
Interim Supply
Over the years the producers negotiated with the dairies the prices for their products. I can remember when fluid milk used to be sold for $3.85 a hundredweight. That was not the price of milk from the ordinary type of farm. This was milk that had been inspected, had been given the bacteria colii test the result of which had to be within certain limits, and had been given the strep test. These controls were applied so as to protect the consumer, the dairy and also the producers. A great deal of money was spent on developing this quota system and raising dairy cattle. Negotiations were carried on over the years to set the proper price, sometimes with great difficulty. The last price I heard about in northern Ontario was something like $6.25 a hundred.
One of the problems which always plagued the fluid milk producers but which was a boon to other segments of the industry was the surplus milk that was produced. I had always thought the farmers might be wise to do what the miners did. When the miners decided to work an eight hour day, they worked eight hours only. They did not work an extra two hours because they were not tired; they decided that eight hours meant eight hours, not 10 or 12 hours, unless they were paid a premium for their extra labour.
What happened in the case of the farmer, Mr. Chairman? He found that having filled his quota the dairy did not require all of the milk. The dairy had over estimated their need and the farmer ended up with a surplus of milk he had to dispose of. It is interesting to note that while I was paying more for chocolate milk than I was for whole milk, this was really surplus milk for which in the early days the farmer was paid only $1.75 a hundred, and for which I as a consumer was paying more than I paid for the fluid milk for which the farmer received $4.25 a hundred. However, that is one of the anomalies of the fluid milk industry.
As the years went by the fluid milk producer found that his ability to increase his production, indeed his need to increase his production if he was to retain an economic unit, meant that he had far more milk available than he had quota to meet. This meant that his surplus of milk increased. I was talking to my brother recently, and he told me that not long ago, when milk sold for $6 a hundred in his local dairy under his quota, he was supplying over 50 per cent of his milk as surplus milk for which he received $2.85 a hundred. This meant he was getting less than $4 a

hundred for the milk that he produced many months of the year.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, hon. members should consider this situation, because the government are now promoting this state of affairs in another way. The milk producers of Ontario, British Columbia, Nova Scotia, indeed most provinces in Canada, have developed a considerable market for fluid milk which has remained relatively stable but has not received the same impetus of growth that you would expect in other fields. This is emphasized by the fact that the farmer can produce a great deal more than he could originally produce.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
One year ago this problem blew up, with the Quebec farmers blocking the highways to draw the public's attention to their plight. The same situation later developed in Ontario, and when the farmers took their tractors out on the roads the government decided, on looking at the problem, that it was in the position to provide subsidies, and that the milk going to the creameries and dairies would run at least at $3.25. That figure has since been raised by federal and provincial supports to $4.25.
The minister made a statement in January saying that the matter was solved and that the farmers could expect no further assistance from the federal government. The price of this milk had been raised to $4.25, and with additional subsidies in the manufacturing field it went to $4.75, although 11 cents from that was deducted. I have always been curious about that 11 cents. I do not know what happens to it, neither do the farmers.
When the proposal to set the price at $4.25 was considered last year the federal government agreed to subsidize the surplus of the fluid milk producers. Within limitations it agreed to pay a subsidy on part of the fluid milk surpluses. That created some havoc, because producers of fluid milk who had originally sold half their production shipped their milk to northern Ontario under dubious sanitary conditions and competed with the producers up there. The whole problem blew up when Mr. Cooper, the president of the dairy council warned that there would be serious repercussions unless the federal government took active steps in the field of milk production to eliminate some of the difficulties.
To protect farmers it was recommended that the price of manufacturing milk be raised to $5.10. The farmers would break even at that figure and make no profit. That

advice was ignored, and the National Dairy Council considered the position of farmers and warned what such a refusal would do. Since then, as the hon. member for Kent (Ont.) has said, the government has taken little constructive action, though it must be aware of the storm centres that are brewing.
The provincial marketing board at Queen's Park has agreed to raise the price of milk to producers by 35 cents; considering that there are 38 quarts in a hundredweight, the net effect ought to be that the consumer will pay one cent more per quart; yet he will pay three cents more. Three cents more has been charged in some areas quite legitimately, but I would not wish it to be thought that such increase benefits farmers. The dairies, by charging this extra 3 cents, have seen a way to blame farmers and the government, and at the same time ease their own difficulties.
In an article from Queen's Park, Don O'Hearn says that the provincial authorities cannot control the situation, and that the Ontario government is in serious difficulties. Probably there will be a consumer outcry which will reduce fluid milk sales in Ontario, with the farmer gaining not one cent.
The minister is not unaware of the situation, because in his own area, Arnprior, 1,000 farmers attended a meeting to protest what is happening. For the sake of his future the minister ought to be interested in the implications of what is happening, because the farmers are not satisfied, and they are not going to be satisfied with the small relief given to them.
In one of its releases the dairy commission, on April 14, talked about price equalization. They said that only manufacturing milk and creamery shippers will be eligible for the subsidy. Furthermore, the commission says- and these remarks apply not to the big shippers shipping 10,000 or 20,000 pounds annually-that should any portion of the fluid milk producer's product be diverted to the manufacturing field, that fluid milk producer will not be eligible for any subsidy on milk that is delivered for manufacturing.
This means that many of the quotas which have been set are unrealistic, as some producers at some times have enormous surpluses. I know that the minister has had problems with quotas, but the position of the farmers is that they will not be able to sell their milk in the manufacturing field. What is the good of that? Quotas have been established, farmers have built up their herds and farms, and yet
April 26, 1967



they will not be able to sell their surpluses in the manufacturing field, since they would be forfeiting the subsidy on that milk.
Let us look at the figures. Taking into account the 11 cents that is deducted, the subsidy will be $1.10. That will bring the price of milk f.o.b. the factory, to the fluid milk producer, to $3.65. That is what the farmer will get for his fluid milk production. It should be borne in mind that the milk to be sold at $3.65 cost that much to produce. That milk was produced under the same conditions as the milk which fetches $6, $6.10, or, in some instances, $6.50. The upshot is that the farmer will produce part of his milk to be sold at $6, part to be sold at $3.65, and the average price he receives will be something less than $4.75.
Clearly, if what I say is correct, and I think it is, a farmer's best interest is to quit the production of fluid milk and go into the manufacturing milk business. The farmer will have his equipment, his investment, his herd, and he will have a guaranteed market for up to 300,000 pounds of milk. He will find he receives the same amount of money while spending far less money on equipment and far less time looking after the operation.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
I have outlined the problem facing the fluid milk producer. It seems that the Canadian Dairy Commission intends to establish quotas for producers of manufacturing milk; it will give quotas only to those who have produced over 10,000 pounds in 1966-67 and will only allow quotas for the following year to those producing over 50,000 pounds of milk. This quota, according to the dairy commission, would be their property. In one case the Ontario government will own the quotas of Ontario farmers and in the other federal government will own them. Now, one can go into the market place as though he were buying or selling a house and put a quota up in a magazine or a daily paper, and ask for quotations on it-"how much am I bid?" This will create chaos. It will mean that everyone who wants to buy his way into the dairy industry will be able to do so but it will be impossible to get into the manufacturing field without a good deal of money, and it will be impossible for young people to get started.
This might be all very well if we did not need farmers. The program put forward by the Liberal government in the last election indicated they were pledged to get rid of the small, uneconomic farm. Well, they have done a good job as far as the cream producers are concerned-such a good job that we now have 23033-976
Interim Supply
to import butter from New Zealand. We are not even fair about our butter imports. I understand that the price of a pound in Great Britain is 40 cents. If the Canadian Dairy Commission were to sell it at the floor price we have established they would earn enough money to subsidize some of the farmers who have been put out of business.
Not very long ago a great deal of cream was produced by small farmers who worked out. When they came home at night they milked two or three cows, separated the milk, fed a couple of pigs and a dozen hens and took their cream to the creamery at the end of the week, thus providing themselves with a small amount of spending money-sometimes it went to the wife as "cream money".
I invite hon. members to look around their ridings and tell me how many people are still milking two or three cows. It is no longer possible to do things in this way. We have discouraged the producers of cream to such an extent that there are very few farmers who still separate the cream on their farms and take it to the local creamery. Their milk is used for manufacture and it is the plant which decides whether it will go into cheese or casein, or into butter. The farmer no longer makes the decision.
I asked the minister to produce the legal documents which authorize him to participate in the manufacturing field. I defy the provincial governments to indicate the constitutional right they have to enter the fluid milk field. This does not apply to manufacturing milk because we are handling fluid milk in the provincial field in the same way as we are handling manufacturing milk in the federal field.
The government may be surprised to find that the farmers are not playing any more. The farm movement in my own area has grown by leaps and bounds since the tractor parades were held in Quebec and Ontario. Membership of both farm organizations has increased rapidly. Membership of one of them has, I believe, increased 15 or 20 times during the last year. This indicates that farmers are now aware that if they get together and make a good case something will be done-that it is not necessary for them to wait until the government is defeated at the polls before action can be taken to find a remedy.
We are being very foolish if we decide to force this type of exercise upon the farmers and try to deal with all these questions in piecemeal fashion. Consider what has happened to the farm machinery inquiry. Today

this is a "dead duck" in Ontario. I had the opportunity of appearing in connection with this inquiry. The provincial authorities said this was a matter within federal jurisdiction and no doubt the federal authorities claim it is a matter for the provinces to deal with. The buck is being passed until the farmer is losing sight of it.
This should not be allowed to happen with regard to dairy policy. I believe the Canadian Dairy Commission should co-operate so closely with the provincial governments that arrangements for dealing with both fluid milk and manufacturing milk can be combined. Ideally, in my opinion, the Canadian Dairy Commission should be able to control the whole operation and utilize this dairy product to such advantage as to remove one of the problems which has always plagued the stabilization board. The board found that whenever the floor price of butter was raised in relation to cheese it ran into difficulty because almost immediately more milk went into butter than into cheese, and a surplus developed. An attempt was made to correct the situation by increasing the amount offered for cheese. Again, the balance was thrown out, simply because the board could not relate its actions to the whole marketing situation. One day the government will be obliged to consider the establishment of a national marketing plan involving the pooling of production from all the provinces whether the product is intended for home consumption or for export.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
They are going to have to come to some co-operative arrangement that will allow them to devise a constructive policy that will take into consideration fluctuations in sales and production and at the same time allow all the farmers in the dairy industry to make a decent living and overcome the cost-price squeeze which, if not overcome, will drive farmers off their land very quickly.
The minister and the country are going to hear a great deal more about this problem before interim supply passes tonight, and I for one would appreciate it if the minister would outline what he has in mind before we spend the next six or eight hours debating this matter.
I think the minister is well aware of the problem. He knows that there are 1,000 farmers in the Ottawa valley meeting in the town of Arnprior to discuss this matter. They are not meeting to discuss the weather; they are

vitally interested in this problem. The minister is also well aware of the fact that these farmers have some influence not only on the political scene but also on the news media. He knows their complaints will receive a very receptive hearing from the average Canadian who is sick and tired of finding the farmers always getting the short end of the stick. City and townspeople are well aware of this because when they drive out into the country on week ends to visit their friends and relatives, they discover that the farmer is not getting the benefit of the increased price which the consumer has to pay. The reason for this falls partly within the jurisdiction of the federal government, and thus is within our purview to review. If we do not get some decision on this matter, or an indication that something is going to be done about it, we would be well advised to stay here and debate interim supply for the next two or three days.

Mr. Chairman, I take the opportunity we are given tonight-really the first-to join the members for Kent and Ti-miskaming (Messrs. Danforth and Peters) in submitting our grievances to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Green).
We would have liked you to hear the voice of our electors, especially that of the leaders of our agricultural organizations, because had it been possible for the presidents of farmers' unions to speak in this house this evening, I feel the minister might sometimes change his mind.
On April 18, we tried to adjourn the business of the house. At that time the leader of the Ralliement Creditiste (Mr. Caouette) wanted to protest without delay against the new dairy policy announced by the minister. He wanted to tell him that his policy was simply antiagricultural.
Mr. Chairman, all the farmers in my district wonder if indeed they are not dealing with an antiagricultural minister.
Every possible representation was made way before the policy was announced. Our organizations did their utmost to influence the minister and obtain from the government, their government, justice and equity, so that the farmer might be able to earn a living as easily, and as honestly as people in industry.
I think the minister has always turned a deaf ear to those appeals. I can see him in his seat tonight and he seems somewhat ashamed to look us straight in the eye. When he visits our agricultural ridings, if he ever does, he
April 26. 1967

will be even more ashamed, because the farmers will show their anger.
The farmers did not ask for anything extraordinary, just for a fair minimum. They asked for $5.10 per hundredweight, which, I think, is a reasonable price. That is what I told the farmers on one occasion. I promised them I would support them completely. After all, we are simply the spokesmen of our large organizations and the minister or the representatives of the Canadian Dairy Commission should have listened to us.
If the minister were to establish the price of manufactured milk on a more rational basis, such as the price of fluid milk, I think this would be the best indication that the minister intends to be fair to the farmers, since the price of fluid milk is always more or less on a level with current prices. I do not know what was the basis used, and we may never know.
Who is responsible for this whole policy? For days on end, before the policy was announced, we tried to pry from the minister the secret he kept to himself, and we were answered only on the day he announced his policy, although he knew very well that all the farmers in our ridings had asked to see us in the preceding weeks. I myself met more than 700 farmers who asked me who was in charge of the dairy policy. I had to tell them that I knew no more than they did.
I think that the minister was partly prevented from disclosing anything by a feeling of embarrassment, because when we heard his announcement we realized that he had a reason to be embarrassed, for he had led us to believe that farmers would certainly find the policy satisfactory.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, we are now seeing the beginning of the farmers' answer, and I hope there will not be a repetition here of what took place in the United States.
I say that the government should be responsible enough to take action before those things happen, for it can certainly not claim that it was not warned in the process of making its decisions.
I am not the one who says that, Mr. Chairman. It is not a member's tale, as the saying goes, because I have here an issue of La Terre de Chez Nous, where one finds an article published following the meeting of the 23033-9761

farmers with the Minister of Agriculture here in Ottawa. I quote:
On April 7, a group of about 20 persons representing member organizations of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture met with the Hon. J. J. Greene in Ottawa, with a view to acquainting him with their views on the 1966-67 dairy policy.
It seems to me that it was only natural that farmers should come and explain their needs to the minister and tell him what they expected from him. It seems to me that that was only natural but, judging from the minister's actions, even before that delegation arrived, the decisions were already made, everything was arranged in advance and not an iota was changed.
I read further from the article:
Mr. Lionel Sorel, president of the C.F.U., and Mr. Leopold Harvey, president of the Quebec Manufacturing Milk Producers Federation, took part in the meeting. Mr. Roger Perreault, a C.F.U. economist, accompanied them. Following is the text of the press release issued by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, after the meeting with the minister.
The minister was not alone, for it says later that he was accompanied by Dr. S. C. Barry, chairman of the Canadian Dairy Commission, and by Mr. S. B. Williams, federal deputy minister of agriculture.
As a matter of fact, that is what I had advised C.F.U. members in my riding to do a week earlier, that is to meet with the minister, to send their representative, to get in touch with the minister in order to influence him and tell him what procedure he should follow before making his statement.
But it has become obvious that the words of the senior officials and those of the farm experts are a little like those of the opposition members in this house when the government has decided on a piece of legislation. The debate may last 5, 10 or 15 days, it does not change a thing. It seems that the legislation is prepared by another group outside parliament, that everything is set and that the ministers have to conform, to agree. That is more or less our impression after five years in the house.
Mr. Chairman, I think that the minister will have to do something and before the end of this session. He should start getting letters because I told all my electors that the only way to protest was to swamp the minister with letters, to bury him under them. And when the minister has received enough letters, he might understand the needs of the farmers because it is the only way to wake him up or bury him forever.

Mr. Chairman, the farmers have been made fun of long enough and I assure you that the fight is not over; on the contrary, it has just begun.
I shall side with the farmers and just wait and see who will win, the farmers or the technicians here who have never even set foot on a farm.
Mr. Chairman, there is a limit to such blackmail. In order to know the views of the farmers of my riding, listen to this further article written by Lionel Saurel, grand president of the Catholic Farmers Union. Here is what he wrote on the editorial page:
After taking numerous steps to obtain a fair dairy policy and, following the announcement of that policy, to have its main deficiencies corrected, the Quebec dairy farmers are greatly disappointed. The general public may have thought that the new policy ensured the farmers a $4.75 guaranteed price, but such is not the case. In spite of the increased funds provided by the state to help dairy farmers through a critical period, the efforts of the government are inadequate to meet the requirements of the dairy farmers, since the minimum assistance asked had been estimated at $180 million.
Now, the new policy provides for $120 million, perhaps $110 million, perhaps even $100 million, because all expenditures have been greatly reduced.
A slight increase has been granted for industrial milk, but quotas have been maintained, when our areas are known to have lost ground for the past three years with regard to dairy farming because of bad weather and illness of our cattle. In some areas, 50 per cent of the herds have been destroyed. And then, the grants have been set according to the quotas of those years.
Imagine, sir, the effect of the new policy in our areas especially. When I went to their meeting, mention was made of $4.75 per hundredweight. They said that the minister would not probably grant more than $4.75 per hundredweight. I said that if the minister granted $4.75 per hundredweight, inasmuch as we already received 25 cents per hundredweight, in Quebec, that would amount to $5. But the department played a real nasty trick on them. It forbade Quebec to give 25 cents. If it grants 25 cents, it will be deducted from the $4.75. This is the most nasty trick that the minister could play on them.
And they say that they want to help agriculture. And this is not all. Before that, there was a subsidy for fluid milk, and it was suggested during the meeting to ask the department to abolish the famous percentage of

120 per cent for surpluses of fluid milk; instead of that, the whole subsidy is abolished on fluid milk.
Well, work it out and you will see, Mr. Chairman, that the farmers are rightly dissatisfied.
And I will now continue Mr. Sorel's article:
The producers of manufacturing milk are not assured that they will be paid a guaranteed price of $4.75 per hundredweight of milk. It was announced in the first place that an amount of 10 cents per hundredweight would be set aside to pay exportation subsidies. Now, the Canadian Dairy Commission has just announced that an amount of 11 cents will be used for that purpose and will be earmarked for the entire production whether or not it comes under quotas-
This is a marvelous thing. Quotas will not be overreached to pay subsidies but the transport costs will be deducted from the entire quantity of milk. Can you see the advantages dwindling away, hypocritically, once again.

-in other words the whole production comes from people subjected to quotas. The result is that producers will receive a subsidy which is substantially less than $1.11 per hundredweight.

The following factors will contribute to reduce the direct subsidy:
(a)	quotas

They have not been consulted at all.
-that quotas were set without prior study of the consequences and without their being consulted.
As it is, the system will result in placing in a very difficult situation those producers who intended last year to expand their farm to increase the efficiency of their operations. Moreover, quotas unfortunately do not take into account the regional damages caused by weather conditions or the losses of the producers as a result of cattle diseases.
That is what I was referring to, Mr. Chairman, because in the constituency of Roberval particularly-I am not fully aware of the situation in other constituencies-we have been sorely tried in these areas.
The new policy is unfair to producers of fluid milk. Last year, the federal government estab-

lished a direct subsidy for part of the fluid milk which was not paid for at the class 1 rate or bottling price. This year, that subsidy is eliminated. As a result, with the new dairy policy, a large number of fluid milk producers will receive a lower unit price per hundredweight than before. This decision is unfair and backward. Furthermore, it will result in an increase of fluid milk prices to an undesirable level.
Even if they are fewer in number, the fact remains that cream producers are being handicapped.
Well, fluid milk producers are not the only victims; cream producers, the cheese producers were also left out.
In many areas of Canada, they have no other choice but to ship their cream to the butter-dairy. The new policy does not enable them to earn an income equal to that of the producers whose milk is processed into butter and powdered milk. The producers whose milk is processed for butter and casein are also in the same situation. On the other hand, it is difficult to understand why the government did not decide to increase the support price for cheese.
Mr. Chairman, I believe the minister received many letters about this from cheese producers, with the support of dairy farmers, asking for more justice for cheese producers, because there is a gap. There is a gap between the price of butter and that of cheese, and I think that it is unfair for factories producing cheese only to absorb that gap themselves.

In the last several years, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture has been pressing for the setting up of formal consultation procedures between the federal government and farm producers' organizations.

At this stage, I would ask the minister to take the information supplied by his technicians, who are not only technicians but practitioners because they live among the farmers 365 days a year and are familiar with production, and to give it to his officials so that they will make out of it a more concrete and more realistic policy for Quebec as well as for the whole of Canada.

I also have a copy of Routine Proceedings for March 22, the day on which the house adjourned for the Easter recess, and on page 5 the top item shows the following outstanding: "Second reading of Bill C-278, an act respecting the occupational training of adults."
When the regulations were brought down by order in council the cabinet knew that the necessary legislation had not been passed by parliament. Yet they went ahead and began spending money under this heading without legal authority for so doing. They by-passed parliament completely.
I have given examples to show how the caucus has been ignored. I have shown how the recommendations of party policy conventions have been ignored. Now it has come to the point at which parliament itself is bypassed. I regret very much that situations of this kind occur from time to time. There are other examples I could mention.
There is the example of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. If he spent more time in Ottawa and less in the riding of Lapointe we might get more legality in the actions he carries on. I have been described as not being a typical English speaking Canadian. I know I am not. When the Minister of Manpower and Immigration spoke in Toronto about four weeks ago I was the only sitting member of parliament who went to hear him. There are 18 sitting members of parliament from Toronto. Seventeen did not go to hear him, and one did. That means I am not typical. If I had been typical I would have been one of those who did not go to hear him.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
Hear, hear.

But I would also point out for the edification of the minister that I am not a typical English speaking Canadian. I have no hesitation in going into any part of Quebec where my people have been living, working, marrying and dying since 1795. They don't have to send R.C.M.P. guards with me when I go into Quebec, nor any men in civilian clothes to protect me from my fellow Canadians when I go. I have always moved with ease among them, and always expect to move with ease among them. But that does not get around the question that hundreds of thousands of English speaking Canadians do not want to enter the province of Quebec. They don't like post office boxes being blown up in their faces. They don't like things going "boom" when they turn on the electric light in private homes. Many English speaking Canadians do not want to enter Quebec, but I never have any hesitation in doing so, never have had and never will, and so I am not a typical English speaking Canadian.
I would like to extend my thanks to another minister who went on a television network the night before I spoke in Lapointe and made the announcement to French network viewers that he would advise me not to go into Quebec. I did not know of that announcement. The trouble is, I went. I never thought to ask him for his advice. I do not think he could save me, even if he tried. I like to stand on my own two feet.
I am going to speak in Hamilton on Friday next. But I do not intend to ask, will it be O.K. with him for me to speak there. I say I can move anywhere in Canada that I wish to go, and I will go any place where I am asked by a responsible organization such as the College of Jonquiere. I enjoy meeting my fellow Canadians from coast to coast, and I hope I will always be able to speak in that vein.
I have taken up as much time as I intend to speak on interim supply, but I intend to speak again on the throne speech address in about two weeks time. I would like to give you a few more details, but there are others who wish to speak tonight. However, it is interesting, and I want to leave this thought with you, that on April 21, Friday last, we had the Leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister exchanging words over titles and referring to the title "Right Honourable."
I might state for your information that last July when I was in London I spent over four

April 26, 1967
Interim Supply
and a half hours with the officials of the Privy Council of the United Kingdom and the Colonies, which is its proper name. There is no such thing as an "Imperial Privy Council." That name is used by, shall I say, colonials and status seekers who wish to create the impression that they belong to something super-super. I am happy to remind you that the Prime Minister, in reply to the Leader of the Opposition, referred to "the Imperial Privy Council, so-called." He did not make the mistake of referring to the Privy Council of the United Kingdom and the Colonies as "Imperial Privy Council."
The thought that I want to leave with you tonight is that my good friend, Lord Thomson of Fleet, approached the right hon. member for Prince Albert, as a matter of fact in St. John's Newfoundland, on a certain visit and asked him if he would recommend him for a title as he, Roy Thomson, was living in Great Britain. The answer he got was a straight question, "Would you accept the governor generalship"? The suppliant was somewhat taken aback by the question and after maybe some three or four seconds thought said, "Well, I would take the governor generalship." Well, that was the end of that. Having been a Conservative candidate in Toronto York Centre in 1953 Roy Thomson did not expect any favours from any other party, so he made inquiry as to how he might acquire a title in Great Britain. He was advised by the people there that because he was a Canadian citizen, under the Canadian Citizenship Act, nobody in Britain would recommend him for a title. It would have to be done by the head of the state where his citizenship was, but it was pointed out that if he became a citizen of the United Kingdom and the Colonies they would be very glad to recommend him for a title.
Therefore, on June 5, 1963, Roy Thomson, as we all know him, applied for United Kingdom citizenship which was granted to him immediately and on January 1, 1964, lo and behold, his name appeared in that list of honoured citizens of the United Kingdom and the Colonies, and he was no more a Canadian citizen.
The Nickle resolution reads, and I have it in my hand:
We, Your Majesty's Most dutiful and loyal subjects, the House of Commons of Canada in Parliament assembled, humbly approach Your Majesty, praying that Your Majesty may be graciously pleased:-
(a) To refrain hereafter from conferring any title of honour or titular distinction upon any of your subjects domiciled or ordinarily resident in Canada-

And down further there is a paragraph at the bottom reading:
A suggestion was made that the titles of "Eight Honourable" and "Honourable" be discontinued, but the suggestion did not meet with the approval of the committee.
I asked the officials of the Privy Council of the United Kingdom and the Colonies in London how it was that when my very good friend, Lord Thomson of Fleet, accepted that title he was forced to yield his Canadian citizenship in order to be nominated by the-
